Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT B. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg., cor EDSA Mapagmahal Street, Diliman, Quezon City LEGAL SERVICE DILG OPINION NO. 19 May 2010 MR. DENNIS F. CORPIN Sangguniang Bayan Member Sta. Maria, Romblon Dear SB Member Corpin: 53 s. 2010 This pertains to your letter seeking our legal opinion regarding the authority of the Local Chief Executive to enter into a contract in behalf of the local government unit. In reply thereto, please be informed that we had already an occasion to answer a similar query in DILG Opinion No. 50 s. 2006. In the said opinion, we opined that in order to bind the LGU concerned, the contract has to be entered into by the LCE upon prior authorization of the sanggunian concerned pursuant to Section 22. (c) of the Local Government Code. Attached herewith is a photocopy of DILG Opinion No. 50 s 2006 for your ready perusal. We hope this settles your concern. Very truly yours, By Authority of the Secretary . . JESUS . DOQU IV Direct r Ill Legal: 12/corz

Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL QOVERNMENT rrancisco Oold Condominium II, EDSA cor. Mapagmahal St. Diliman, Quezon City 50 OFFICE OF UNDERSECRETARY FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT 06 December 2006 ENGR. MIGUELIVA V. TOMALES MI'DC/ BAC Chairman Luisiana, Laguna Dear Engr. Tomales: 'Illis refers to your letter requesting our legal opinion on whether or not in issuing the authority to enter into a contract, the Sangguniang Bayan of Luisiana has the authority to review the actions taken by the BAC or to review the previous proceedings of the BAC. You stated that the Municipal Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) of that municipality had already conducted a bidding for the Consultancy Services on the preparation of a Feasibility Study on the Luisiana Waterworks System Improvement Project. Applying the procedures provided for in procuring consultancy services under RA 9184 (An Act Providing for the Modernization, Standardization and Regulation of the Procurement Activities of the Qovemment and For Other Purposes), the BAC already determined a winning bidder for the said project. In view of the need for the Mayor to enter into a contract with the winning bidder, the Mayor wrote the Sangguniang Bayan requesting for an authorization to enter into the contract. "Ihe Sangguniang Bayan acted thereon by initiating a physical evaluation with the other members of the BAC regarding the eligibility documents submitted by the highest rated responsible bidder. Hence, your query. In reply thereto, at the outset, please be informed that the issue raised would involve pertinent provisions of two different laws, namely: RA 7160, otherwise Known as the Local Government Code, and RA 9184, which took effect on 26 January 2003, otherwise Known as An Act Providing for the Modernization, Standardization and Regulation of the Procurement Activities of the Government and For Other Purposes. It bears stressing that pursuant to Section 22 Of the Local Government Code, Local Government Units (LOU), namely: provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays, are conferred with corporate powers, one among which is to enter into contracts. Said contracts are to be entered into by the Local Chief Executive of the LGU concerned. In relation thereto, under paragraph (c) of the said Section of the Local Government Code, it is provided that "no contract may be entered into by the Local Chief Executive in behalf of the Local Government Unit without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned. A legible copy of such contract shall be

-2- posted at a conspicuous place in the provincial capitol or the city, municipal or barangay hall". On the other hand, RA 9184 made it a declared policy of the State Lo promote the ideals of good governance in all its branches, departments, agencies, subdivisions and instrumentalities, including government-owned or controlled corporations and Local Government Units. Accordingly, said law mandated that all procurements of infrastructure projects, goods and consulting services by the abovementioned government entities, including LGUs, shall always comply with the requirement of competitive bidding. it is noted that these two laws (KA 7160 and RA 9184) were enacted on different time and for different purposes. KA 7160 was enacted for local governance, while KA 9184 was enacted for the purpose of setting the rules and procedures in procurement by government entities covered therein, including LCiUs. With respect to RA 9184, Section 76 thereof provides for the repeal of Title Six, 600K II of KA 7160. Title Six of said law, which is the Property and Supply Management in the Local Government Units covers Sections 355 to 386, inclusive. At this point, it is worth mentioning that the Republic of the Philippines observes a Presidential Form of government. In this form of government, fundamental powens of the State are lodged by the Constitution to the three (3) branches of government, namely: the Executive, the Legislative, and the Judiciary. The Executive branch is charged with the execution of laws; the Legislative branch is charged with the enactment of laws; and the Judiciary, with interpretation of laws. Each branch is supreme in its own jurisdiction. The Constitution does not allow interference of one branch to the other. Should there be such interference, the Judiciary will not hesitate to invalidate the action of the encroaching branch, in complete adherence to the principle of separation of branch and separation of powers. Executive branch is headed by the President, the Legislative branch is headed by Congress and the Judiciary is headed by the Supreme Court. A Local Government Unit (LOU) falls under the Executive branch. Accordingly, all officials and employees of the LOU are part of the Executive branch. In this regard, it is equally important to note that Section 48 of the Local Government Code mandates that the Sangguniang panlalawigan with respect to provinces, the Sangguniang I'anlungsod with respect to cities, the Sangguniang Bayan with respect to municipalities, and the Sangguniang Barangay with respect to barangays, are the legislative bodies in the local government units. In the case of Magtajas vs. Pryce Properties, Inc. (O.K. No. II 1097, 20 July 1994), the Supreme Court declared that the different sanggunians of the LGUs are exercising delegated legislative powers. Hence, the power to enact a national or regional law is lodged with Congress, while the power to enact ordinances is delegated to the different

sanggunians. An ordinance is a local law applicable only within the territorial jurisdiction of the concerned I-QU. From the foregoing, it is thus clear that while there is no separation of branch at the LGU level, it belonging to the Executive branch, there is, however, present, the principle of separation of powers and functions such that the Local Chief Executive performs full executive functions, while the sanggunian, composed of the Vice Chief Executive as the Presiding Officer, the regular members and sectoral representatives, perform legislative functions. In order, however, io provide check and balance at the local level, there are certain powers of an LGU that can only be done through the interdependence, meaning, through the simultaneous actions of both the Local Chief Executive and the Sanggunian. An example of this is the power of the LOU to enter into a contract. As discussed above, it is noted that the Mayor cannot enter into any contract by himself alone and binding the LOU. Prior authorization from the sanggunian is a requirement Of law in order to bind the LGU under the contract. Along this line, it is worthy cf note that procurement of goods, services and infrastructure projects are clearly executive functions. Neither KA 7160 nor KA 9184 provided interaction between the Executive and the Legislative functions. It is solely an executive function. Significantly, it may be worth to note that Section I I, Article V of KA 9184 expressly mandated that each procuring entity, including the LOU, shall establish a single Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) for its procurement. The function of the BAC is clearly an executive function, assisting, as it does, the determination of the winning bidder. Once the qualified winning bidder has already been determined, and the Notice of Award therefor has already been given, the LCE shall now enter into a contract with the winning bidder. However, in order to bind the LGU concerned, the contract has to be entered into by the LCE upon prior authorization of the Sanggunian concerned pursuant to Section 22 (c) of the Local Government Code. Accordingly, the sanggunian, under the cloak of providing authorization for the Mayor to enter into a contract, cannot encroach into the functions of the Executive office of the Mayor by duplicating what the BAC has already done. The extent of authority of the Sanggunian is only to authorize the Mayor in order to bind the LGU under the contract and not to act as another BAC which would only duplicate the process made by the BAC to the prejudice of the expeditious prosecution of the procurement. All the foregoing considered, we are of the view that it is not proper and legal for the Sangguniang Bayan of that municipality to review the actions or proceedings of the BACO in effect duplicating the statutorily mandated powers and functions of the BAC, as it would be violative of the laws aforementioned and the principle of separation of powers and functions. Finally, if the Sangguniang Bayan believes that the proceedings in the BAC was tainted with some anomalies that led to the awarding of the

-4- contract to a winning bidder, then the former has ail the legal remedies to i have the contract rescinded before the courts or to institute appropriate administrative, criminal or civil suits against the BAC members and any other person who participated in the illegal transactions. moreover, if the losing bidder believes that the contract should have been awarded to him instead of the winning bidder, then the former should have availed of the protest mechanism as provided for under Sections 55- 58, Rule XVII of the IRK-A of the Government Procurement Act (KA 9184). We hope we have enlightened you on the matter. Very truly yours, USE-C WENCEUIO V. Officer-in-Charge, Dill) Legal: 43/1.a cc.• Director Leonilo B. Lariosa DILO Redlional Office mo.
